new_statements.quote: It may here be remarked that, as an almost invariable rule, words of two or three syllables are accented on the last. Hence it will generally be found unnecessary in these notes to indicate accent by any distinguishing mark. [...] * This vowel sound is similar to that of u in but, yet always unaccented.
new_statements.citation: Stilson, Lyman. 1866. Brief notice of the Kemi language, spoken by a tribe in Arrakan, Farther India. Journal of the American Oriental Society 8: 213-226.
new_statements.locator: p. 219 (Article V, section on sounds, immediately after the vowel and final-consonant lists); footnote * on the same page
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words almost without exception; the reduced (schwa-like) presyllable vowel is never accented. Consistent with So-Hartmann 2001:136-137 (Mro ka- 'an unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable') and Hornéy 2012:39 (minor-syllable vowel 'much shorter duration'), i.e. iambic sesquisyllabic prominence on the major/root syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost invariable rule' -- exceptions implied but none listed. Footnote p.219: the reduced vowel 'a as in apology' (the minor-syllable schwa) is 'always unaccented'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from a missionary sketch and spelling-book/reader data (wordlist and sentences); the rule is stated for polysyllabic words generally, including prefixed verbs (ta-, a-, ma- 'frequently occurring prefixes to verbs', p.224). The language is tonal per Hornéy 2012 (H/L, root melodies), which Stilson does not mark or mention; 'accent' here is impressionistic 19th-century stress-accent.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from Stilson 1866 on 'Kemi', the Khami of the northern Arakan plains ('not found farther south than about twenty miles north of Akyab', distinct from the 'Koomis'), data collected 1841-42. ISO 639-3 CR 2011-037 identifies the Arakan-plains 'Awa Khami' with the Wakung sub-group of Mro-Khimi [cmr] (Kyauktaw, Buthidaung, Mrauk-U, Ponnagyun), and Lotven 2021/2023 explicitly equates Stilson's Kemi with Mro-Khimi; the ex-code Khumi Awa [cka] (Glottolog khum1250, now merged) is the same variety. Identity with mroc1235 therefore rests on geography plus Lotven's equation, not on a lexical match; Stilson's 'woman' nāuṅ-pūi-dī ~ Hornéy Wakun /nɛ́pýdí/ but the same root exists in Kanise Khumi. Shafer 1944 'Khimi' is Khumi proper (khum1248), not this language. The modern primary phonology (Hornéy 2012, Wakun dialect) is silent on stress; So-Hartmann 2001 (Wakung) gives only the implicit 'unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable' for ka-.

sources.note: Second-hand: 'Stilson (1866: 19), writing on Kemī (or Mro-Khimi), discussed the prosodic phonology of the language in terms of the more familiar stress-accent systems found in Europe: "as an almost invariable rule, words of two or three syllables are accented on the last."' Equates Stilson's Kemi with Mro-Khimi.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2011. Change Request 2011-037: merge Chin, Khumi Awa [cka] into Chin, Mro [cmr]; rename Mro-Khimi.
sources.note: Identity evidence only: the Arakan-plains 'Awa Khami' of the 1931 Census = Wakung sub-group of Mro-Khimi (Kyauktaw, Buthidaung, Mrauk-U, Ponnagyun etc.).

sources.citation: So-Hartmann, Helga. 2009. A descriptive grammar of Daai Chin. STEDT Monograph 7. Berkeley.
sources.note: p.38 compares Daai/Mro/Lemi presyllables: 'Mro and Lemi having a bit more syllabicity in the form of a reduced schwa vowel'; Daai (not Mro) described as iambic presyllable+stressed main syllable. p.31: Shafer 1944 is based on Khumi (Francis's St Matthew), not Mro-Khimi.

sources.citation: Hornéy, Christina Scotte. 2012. A phonological analysis of Mro Khimi. MA thesis, University of North Dakota (Scholarly Commons Theses 4108), xi+85 pp.

sources.note: Silent on stress: the strings 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur in the text layer. Ch.4 p.39: minor-syllable prefixes have a surface schwa 'which has a much shorter duration than vowels in other syllables'; p.42 word minimally a major syllable which the minor syllable may precede but not follow. Ch.5: two tones H/L, affixes toneless, falling pitch phrase-final only.

sources.citation: Tan, Cheng Hooi. 2022. Minor syllables in Kanise Khumi. MA thesis, Payap University; and Ikeda, Elissa 2022 in JSEALS Special Publication 8.
sources.note: Second-hand only: Tan quotes So-Hartmann 2001 on Mro Khimi ka- 'It is an unstressed prefix, but with the distinct vowel [a~ʌ]'; Ikeda/Tan summarise Hornéy 2012 (minor syllables much shorter, toneless affixes). No placement rule for Mro-Khimi.

sources.note: pp.136-137 (Mro = Wakung Mro-Khimi): 'Mro has yet another prefix, ka-, that is phonetically very distinct from k- [kə-]. It is an unstressed prefix, or pre-syllable, but with the distinct vowel [a~ʌ].' Implicit only: prefixes/presyllables unstressed, root syllable stressed; no general placement rule.
